reasons: Every Atlassian OAuth app gets one 65,000-point hourly API quota shared across all the sites it is used on. On a shared app, other developers' traffic counts against the same quota, and when it runs out every request fails until the hour resets. Your own app gives you your own quota.
Your users see your app name on Atlassian's consent screen instead of a third party's.

Composio's Jira toolkit page and its managed-OAuth directory both say Composio provides a managed Jira app, so you can test with no setup. An older Composio Jira credentials guide says the opposite; trust the toolkit page.

verdict.summary: Self-serve, no approval needed to go live. You can register the app and connect your own Jira in under an hour, and open it to all your users the same day by switching on sharing. Until Atlassian reviews the app, users see a 'not yet reviewed by Atlassian' warning on the consent screen, and Atlassian publishes no timeline for that review.

timeToProduction.label: Same day with a warning on the consent screen. Removing the warning: Atlassian review, no published timeline

verdict.mainBlocker: The 'not yet reviewed by Atlassian' warning your users see until Atlassian reviews the app, and customer sites whose admins block user-installed apps.

stages.name: Register the app
limits: There is no API for creating Atlassian OAuth apps. This stage has to be done in the browser.

steps.title: Create an OAuth 2.0 integration
steps.detail: In the Atlassian developer console, choose Create, then OAuth 2.0 integration. Name it after your product: this is the name your users see on the consent screen. Pick a grant type: resource-level limits each user's consent to the sites they select; account-level covers every site the user has.
steps.humanReason: Requires signing in to your Atlassian account, and Atlassian offers no API for app creation.

steps.title: Set the callback URL
steps.detail: Open Authorization, choose OAuth 2.0 (3LO) and paste Composio's redirect URI. Copy it from your Composio dashboard when you create the Jira auth config. Do not copy it from older guides: Composio's Jira credentials page shows a /api/v1/ path that its own knowledge base calls legacy.

preparedValues.label: Callback URL
preparedValues.value: Copy from Composio: Auth Configs > Create Auth Config > Jira > OAuth2

steps.title: Add APIs and scopes
steps.detail: Open Permissions and add the Jira API. Add Jira Software only if you use sprint or board tools, and Jira Service Management only if you use service desk tools. Then choose Configure to add the individual scopes. Add only the scopes your agent's tools need: an app can request at most 50, and the consent screen fails if you request a scope you haven't added here.

steps.title: Copy the Client ID and Secret
steps.detail: Open Settings and copy the Client ID and Secret. Treat the secret like a password: it goes into Composio and nowhere else.
steps.humanReason: The secret should only pass from your console to Composio.

stages.name: Connect it in Composio and test
limits: While the app is private, only you (the owner) can authorize it.

steps.title: Create the Jira auth config in Composio
steps.detail: Create an OAuth2 auth config for Jira with your Client ID, Client Secret and the same scopes you added in Atlassian, including offline_access. Without offline_access (and audience=api.atlassian.com, which Composio sets), you get no refresh token and the connection dies within an hour.

steps.title: Connect your own Jira site
steps.detail: Start a connection with your Jira site's base URL, https://<your-site>.atlassian.net, approve the consent screen and run one read tool (for example, list projects) to confirm it works.
steps.humanReason: You approve the consent screen with your own Atlassian account.

stages.name: Open it to your users

duration.label: Same day, plus engineering time if you store personal data

limits: Users see a 'not yet been reviewed by Atlassian' warning until Atlassian reviews the app. They can still continue.
One 65,000-point hourly API quota shared across all your customers' sites. Exceeding it blocks every request until the next hour.
Refresh tokens expire after 90 days without use; the user then has to reconnect.

steps.title: Switch on sharing
steps.detail: Open Distribution, choose Edit and set the status to Sharing. Fill in the vendor name and privacy policy URL. Answer whether your app stores personal data; if it does, you must confirm you have implemented Atlassian's personal data reporting API.
steps.humanReason: The vendor details and the personal-data answer are declarations your company makes to Atlassian.

steps.title: Report personal data (only if you store it)
steps.detail: Apps that store Atlassian users' personal data must report those accounts through the personal data reporting API, by default every 7 days (follow the Cycle-Period header if it returns a different period).

steps.title: Optional: request Atlassian's review to remove the warning
steps.detail: Follow Atlassian's third-party integration listing process. You do not need a Marketplace listing to ask for review. Atlassian publishes no review timeline; the most recent public wait-time reports are from 2020 and describe delays of weeks to months.
steps.humanReason: A submission made on behalf of your company.

requirements.title: Vendor name and privacy policy URL
requirements.detail: Required before you can switch on sharing. An Atlassian staff member described them as mostly form fields, but use your real company and policy.

requirements.title: Personal data reporting
requirements.detail: If your app stores Atlassian users' personal data, you must report those accounts every 7 days by default.

requirements.title: At most 50 scopes per app
requirements.detail: Request only the scopes your tools use. Adding scopes later makes existing users consent again.

requirements.title: Refresh tokens rotate and expire after 90 days of inactivity
requirements.detail: Each refresh issues a new refresh token. A user who goes 90 days without the connection being used must reconnect.

blockers.title: Callback URL mismatch
blockers.symptom: The consent screen errors before the user can approve.
blockers.fix: Make the callback URL in Atlassian identical to the redirect URI in your Composio auth config. Copy it from the Composio dashboard, not from an older guide.

blockers.title: Connection stops working after about an hour
blockers.symptom: Tool calls start failing with auth errors shortly after connecting.
blockers.fix: No refresh token was issued. Add offline_access to the scopes in both Atlassian and Composio, then reconnect.

blockers.title: Consent fails because of scopes
blockers.symptom: The consent screen errors, or tools fail with permission errors.
blockers.fix: Every scope Composio requests must be added in the developer console, and the total must stay at or under 50.

blockers.title: Customer's admin blocks user-installed apps
blockers.symptom: The consent screen tells the user their admin has disabled end-user installs.
blockers.fix: The customer's Atlassian admin must allow user-installed apps (admin.atlassian.com > Security > Connected apps). The control is all-or-nothing; admins cannot allow a single app.

blockers.title: Every customer gets 429 errors at once
blockers.symptom: All Jira tool calls fail with 429 Too Many Requests until the top of the hour.
blockers.fix: The app's shared 65,000-point hourly quota is used up. Cut call volume, or ask Atlassian for per-tenant quotas, which needs a review.

agentCan: Pick the minimum scopes for the Composio Jira tools you use
Prepare every value to paste into the developer console
Create the Composio auth config through Composio's API once you give it the Client ID and Secret through a secure channel
Draft the privacy-policy section about Jira data, and the vendor details
Write the personal data reporting job if you store personal data
Draft the note your customers' admins need if they block user-installed apps
youMust: Sign in and create the app in the developer console (Atlassian has no API for this)
Decide and declare whether your app stores personal data
Approve the first consent screen to test
Submit Atlassian's review, if you want the warning removed

unknowns.whyItMatters: Atlassian asks you to pick one when you create the app.

unknowns.question: When Composio stores the tokens, who meets Atlassian's personal data reporting requirement?
unknowns.whyItMatters: Switching on sharing asks you to confirm you've implemented the reporting API if your app stores personal data.

Atlassian requires apps that store users' personal data to report those accounts through its personal data reporting API. Does Composio store personal data for Jira connections in a way we need to report, and does Composio report it for custom apps? Thanks.

unknowns.whyItMatters: Decides when the consent-screen warning goes away.

claims.text: OAuth 2.0 apps are created in the developer console via Create > OAuth 2.0 integration; the Client ID and Secret are under Settings.
Apps choose an account-level grant (one consent covers multiple sites) or a resource-level grant (consent limited to the sites the user selects).
